findings.text: Ashland Avenue & Cullerton Street had 18 injury crashes in police records since 2021-10-31: 1 person killed.
At the U.S. DOT's values that harm costs about $1.2 million a year (injury crashes only).
What these crashes have in common is not compared with the rest of the city: it has no screened priority junctions to compare against.

The raised island targets pedestrian injury crashes with CMF 0.685 (31.5% reduction) from national studies, expected to avoid about 0.2 crashes a year, including 0.19 injury crashes avoided per year, worth $65,000 per year in harm avoided.
Cost covers is not stated with break-even cost $455,000 against $65,000 per year in harm avoided.
Rectangular Rapid Flashing Beacons would avoid about 0.3 crashes a year, worth $97,000 a year.

Best alternative is Rectangular Rapid Flashing Beacons at low-cost scale with FHWA-cited evidence and CMF 0.526, expected to avoid 0.28 injury crashes avoided per year worth $97,000 per year with break-even $684,000.
The Chicago Department of Transportation (CDOT) is responsible for South Ashland Avenue and West Cullerton Street.

answers.answer: The appraised target is 0.6 pedestrian injury crashes per year, and the island is estimated to avoid 0.19 injury crashes avoided per year; relevance is limited to that subset, which is why the verdict remains proceed rather than a broader claim.

Rectangular Rapid Flashing Beacons as best alternative would avoid 0.28 injury crashes avoided per year versus 0.19 injury crashes avoided per year for the island, but the island still shows positive expected harm avoided and the appraisal retains proceed.
Cost covers is not stated and break-even cost is $455,000, so proceeding assumes final cost will be weighed against $65,000 per year in harm avoided before funds commit.
Pavement Friction Management would avoid about 0.4 crashes a year worth $129,000 a year for wet-road patterns, a separate pattern the island does not target.

Responsibility is attributed to the Chicago Department of Transportation (CDOT) for South Ashland Avenue and West Cullerton Street, and the ready draft request letter provides the path to confirm commitment.

cases.letter:
To: the District Department of Transportation (DDOT)
Subject: Request for safety study and signal improvements at 22nd Street NW & L Street NW

Dear colleagues at DDOT,

We are writing about the junction of 22nd Street Northwest & L Street Northwest.

The city's open record for the 5 years from 31 October 2021 shows 38 crashes including 13 injury crashes. The record of who was hurt includes 2 pedestrians injured, 3 cyclists injured, and motorists, with 0 people killed listed. In the U.S. DOT's official values for the cost of crashes (2024 dollars), the yearly cost of the harm is $0.9 million. The records do not show recent safety work in this period, but list NHS - Federal Aid Pavement Restoration - NHPP Streets in 2026 as the latest recorded safety project and NHS - Federal Aid Pavement Restoration - NHPP Streets in 2027 as planned.

The site is listed as a city priority location. We respectfully ask you to carry out a safety study at this junction and, on the roads you are responsible for, to include the fixes noted below where the study shows they fit, using the plain names the city uses.

Longer yellow signal times, which would need a check that there is an entry on yellow or red and that the current yellow plus all-red time is below the ITE recommended practice, is expected to prevent injury crashes.

Reflective backplates on the traffic signals, which would need a check for an entry on yellow or red, is expected to prevent injury crashes.

The city record shows Leading Pedestrian Interval signals are already in place. The earlier program's effect was not shown and we ask for a different approach based on the independent checks above.

Thank you for your work and consideration.

Yours sincerely,

[Your name]
[Your organisation or address]

* Longer yellow signal times. This is expected to prevent about 0.50 injury crashes per year, avoiding about $176,000 in harm per year. It would pay for itself if it costs under $1.2 million. cases.letter:
To: the Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT)
Subject: Request for safety study at Beacon Avenue South & South Webster Street

Dear colleagues at SDOT,

We are writing to ask each road owner to carry out a safety study at the junction of Beacon Avenue South & South Webster Street and to consider fixes on the roads it is responsible for.

The official record for the 5 years from 31 October 2021 shows 24 crashes, of which 10 were injury crashes. One person was killed. No breakdown by pedestrians or cyclists injured was recorded. Valued in the U.S. DOT's official values for the cost of crashes (2024 dollars), the harm averages $0.7 million per year. No recent safety work is recorded for this junction in the period.

On the roads it controls - 32nd Avenue South, 33rd Avenue South, Beacon Avenue South, and South Webster Street - we ask SDOT to assess:

- flashing beacons at the crosswalk, which is FHWA-cited evidence and is expected to prevent 0.2 pedestrian injury crashes per year, avoiding about $65,000 in harm per year, and would pay for itself under $0.5 million;

- better street lighting, which would need a site check to confirm the corner has no street lighting now, and is expected to prevent 0.3 injury crashes in darkness per year, avoiding about $96,000 in harm per year, and would pay for itself under $0.7 million.

Please let us know the outcome of the study and next steps.

Yours sincerely,
[Your name]
[Your organisation or address]

Underreporting bias: police injury-only dataset misses near-misses and non-injury pedestrian conflicts that medians address; a concrete refuge could prevent future severe harm not yet reflected in the thin record.
